The proposed URL is the real Wikipedia redirect with the apostrophe dropped. One character separates it from a live page.

1) Proposed URL: `curl -sI https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/418_Im_a_teapot` -> HTTP/2 404 (real 404 from mw-web, content-type text/html).

2) Correct form returns 200: `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/418_I%27m_a_teapot` -> HTTP/2 200 (also 200 with the literal unencoded apostrophe). The MediaWiki API confirms it is a redirect: {"from": "418 I'm a teapot", "to": "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol", "tofragment": "Commands and replies"}.

3) Not DELETED. API query for title "418 Im a teapot" (no apostrophe) returns "missing": "" and `list=logevents&letitle=418 Im a teapot` returns an EMPTY log array — no creation, deletion, or move ever. That exact string never existed as a page or redirect. By contrast, the apostrophe title's log shows: create 2022-02-03T04:04:32Z, comment "Redirected page to [[Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol#Commands and replies]]".

4) Not BLOCKED. The same User-Agent from the same client got HTTP 200 on sibling paths on the same host in the same minute (/wiki/HTTP_418 -> 200, /wiki/Hyper_Text_Coffee_Pot_Control_Protocol -> 200). Wikipedia is not refusing automated access here.

5) Not a fragment problem. The proposed URL has no fragment, and the base path itself 404s. The anchor id="Commands_and_replies" does exist on the target article, so the redirect's fragment is valid too.

6) The target answers the question. The canonical article https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyper_Text_Coffee_Pot_Control_Protocol (200, pageid 1623162, last-modified 2026-08-11) contains: "418 I'm a teapot — The HTCPCP server is a teapot but was requested to brew coffee", plus RFC 2324 (Larry Masinter, April 1 1998, April Fools' joke) and the 2017 "save 418" movement (Mark Nottingham / IETF HTTPBIS).

RECOMMENDED REPLACEMENT URL (no special characters, safest for the fetcher): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyper_Text_Coffee_Pot_Control_Protocol
Alternate clean redirect that also works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_418 (API confirms it redirects to the same article).

Boundary note for accuracy on air: this is MALFORMED rather than INVENTED only because a real slug differing by a single apostrophe exists and resolves. The research agent did not fabricate the topic — status code 418 is genuine (RFC 2324) and Wikipedia does cover it. Do not characterize this as a hallucinated source; characterize it as a punctuation-mangled URL. Practical caution: the apostrophe form works but is fragile in pipelines, so prefer the Hyper_Text_Coffee_Pot_Control_Protocol path.

Five independent checks all agree the title never existed on English Wikipedia.

1) HTTP status: `curl -sI` and a GET both return HTTP/2 404 from Wikipedia's own app servers (server: mw-web.eqiad..., content-type: text/html). This is a genuine article-not-found page, not a 403/429/bot wall, so BLOCKED is ruled out. No fragment is involved — the bare base path 404s.

2) MediaWiki API, title lookup with redirect resolution: `action=query&titles=Variable_declarator&prop=info&redirects` returns `{"ns":0,"title":"Variable declarator","missing":""}` — the page does not exist AND no redirect originates from that slug. So it is not a live redirect target and not MOVED.

3) Log check (rules out DELETED): `list=logevents&letitle=Variable%20declarator` returns `{"logevents":[]}` — empty. Same for the "Variable Declarator" capitalization. Sanity check that this query does surface deletions: the identical call on `Wikipedia:Sandbox/Test` returns three `type":"delete"` entries (2007-2008), so a deletion would have shown. There is no delete log, no move log, no creation log for this title.

4) Wayback Machine (independent of Wikipedia): `archive.org/wayback/available?url=en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_declarator` returns `"archived_snapshots": {}`, and the CDX index returns zero rows. Control query on `en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declarator` returns real captures (20161017115157, 20231213131808, 20241225071029, all status 200), proving the CDX query form works. Nobody ever archived this URL, consistent with it never having rendered.

5) Nearby-title enumeration: `list=allpages&apprefix=Variable dec` returns only "Variable decelerations", "Variable declaration" (pageid 945122), "Variable declarations". No "declarator" variant in any form. A full-text search for `insource:"variable declarator"` returns 0 total hits across all of en.wikipedia — the exact phrase appears nowhere, so this is not a mangled version of an existing title (rules out MALFORMED).

Why the model produced it: "declarator" is a real term (C/C++ grammar; the ESTree AST node for JS is literally named `VariableDeclarator`), so the slug looks plausible — the classic invented-URL pattern of composing a real technical term into a Wikipedia path that was never used.

Nearest real pages (all HTTP 200, offered as substitutes, NOT as the moved location of this URL, which has none): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_(computer_programming) — the target of the existing redirect "Variable declaration"; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declarator (a 726-byte stub, C/C++ oriented); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript_syntax — the only one that actually touches the proposed question, with 12 mentions of "hoist" and 2 of "block scope". Caveat for the episode: none of these is an authoritative source on `let` vs `var`; MDN's let/var reference or the ECMAScript spec is the correct citation.

FIVE INDEPENDENT CHECKS, ALL NEGATIVE.

1) Direct fetch: `curl -sI` with a real browser UA returns HTTP/2 404 (content-length 88148 = MDN's SPA 404 page, cache-control: no-store). No fragment is involved, so this is a genuine base-page 404 — the "base 200 + bad fragment" nuance does not apply.

2) The parent path is also fake. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Protocols -> 404. There is no "Protocols" segment anywhere in MDN's HTTP tree. Confirmed against the source of truth: GitHub api mdn/content /files/en-us/web/http/ contains exactly three entries — dir `guides`, dir `reference`, file `index.md`. No `protocols`.

3) No redirect exists, which rules out MOVED. MDN's canonical files/en-us/_redirects.txt (17,576 entries, covering every URL reorganization in MDN history) contains ZERO lines matching "Web/HTTP/Protocols", ZERO lines containing "/Protocols/" at all, and ZERO HTTP-version-style pages matching ^/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/.*1[._]1. That file demonstrably does capture real reorgs: /Web/HTTP/Basics_of_HTTP/Evolution_of_HTTP correctly 301s to /Web/HTTP/Guides/Evolution_of_HTTP. A moved page would have an entry; this one has none.

4) No archived copy ever existed, which rules out DELETED. Wayback CDX returned zero captures for the exact URL and zero for the prefix developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Protocols* . CONTROL TEST proving the query method works: the same CDX query against the real (since-moved) .../Basics_of_HTTP/Evolution_of_HTTP returned captures dated 20161224, 20170202, 20170702 (all 200). The server serves us fine; it simply has no such page. MDN's own search API for "HTTP/1.1" returns no version-dedicated page (closest hits: Connection_management_in_HTTP_1.x, Guides/Messages).

REAL SOURCE THAT ANSWERS THE QUESTION: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Evolution_of_HTTP (verified 200). It states: "HTTP/1.1 was updated again in 2022 with RFC 9110... all of HTTP was revised and is now split into: semantics (RFC 9110), caching (RFC 9111) applying to all HTTP versions, and HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112), HTTP/2 (RFC 9113), HTTP/3 (RFC 9114)."

RFC FACT-CHECK (fetched rfc-editor.org full text): RFC 9110 = "HTTP Semantics", STD 97, June 2022, obsoletes 2818/7230/7231/7232/7233/7235/7538/7615/7694. RFC 9112 = "HTTP/1.1", STD 99, June 2022, obsoletes 7230. RFC 2616 = obsolete combined HTTP/1.1 spec. EPISODE CAUTION: the precise answer is that semantics are defined by RFC 9110 (version-independent, not HTTP/1.1-specific), while RFC 9112 defines HTTP/1.1 message syntax/parsing. Lineage: RFC 2068 (1997) -> RFC 2616 (1999) -> RFC 7230-7235 (2014) -> RFC 9110/9112 (2022).

NO WIKIPEDIA PAGE ANSWERS THE QUESTION AT ALL: insource:/allSettled/ across enwiki mainspace returned totalhits=1, the "JavaScript" article, and only as one passing clause: "The methods introduced are: Promise.race, Promise.all, Promise.allSettled and Promise.any."
